pharm: A spore-forming, lactic-acid-producing bacterium historically named Lactobacillus sporogenes and now correctly classified as Bacillus coagulans. As a probiotic it transiently colonizes the gut to restore microbial balance, used mainly for diarrhea and other gastrointestinal complaints. It is marketed as a dietary supplement, not an FDA-approved drug.

summary: Lactobacillus sporogenes is the historical name for Bacillus coagulans, a spore-forming probiotic that produces L(+) lactic acid. Because it forms spores it is heat- and acid-resistant, survives gastric passage well, and is shelf-stable. It is used as a probiotic dietary supplement to help restore intestinal flora and as supportive therapy for acute and antibiotic-associated diarrhea, some functional GI disorders, and as an adjunct after antibiotics. It is regulated as a dietary supplement rather than an FDA-approved medicine, so doses (expressed in colony-forming units, CFU) and quality vary by product. It is generally well tolerated; the main safety concern is rare invasive infection (bacteremia) in severely immunocompromised patients or those with central venous catheters.
indications: Probiotic supplementation to support/restore intestinal microbial balance
Supportive management of acute infectious and antibiotic-associated diarrhea
Symptom support in some functional bowel disorders (e.g., bloating, irritable bowel symptoms) - supplement use, not an approved drug indication

moa: As a probiotic, Bacillus coagulans (Lactobacillus sporogenes) is ingested as dormant spores that germinate in the intestine. There it produces L(+) lactic acid and bacteriocin-like substances that lower luminal pH and inhibit pathogenic bacteria, competes with pathogens for nutrients and adhesion sites, and may modulate the gut immune response and reinforce the intestinal barrier. These effects transiently restore a favorable balance of intestinal flora; the organism does not permanently colonize the gut.

Critically ill patients or those with central venous catheters (rare risk of probiotic bacteremia)

Signs of infection in immunocompromised or central-line patients

preg: Probiotics such as Bacillus coagulans are generally considered to be of low risk in pregnancy because they act locally in the gut, but specific safety data are limited. Use during pregnancy under the advice of a healthcare professional.
lact: Probiotics are generally considered compatible with breastfeeding and are not expected to reach the infant systemically, but formal data are limited. Use during breastfeeding under the advice of a healthcare professional.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed in renal impairment. Use caution in severely immunocompromised patients regardless of renal status because of the rare risk of invasive infection.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed in hepatic impairment. Standard caution regarding invasive infection applies to severely ill/immunocompromised patients.

moderate: Systemic antibiotics - may reduce the viability of the live organism; separate dosing by about 2 hours
Immunosuppressants - theoretical increased risk of probiotic-related infection in heavily immunosuppressed patients
minor: Antifungal agents may also affect viability if taken together
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; acid-stable spores survive gastric passage.

serious: Probiotic bacteremia/sepsis (rare, essentially limited to severely immunocompromised or central-line patients)
emergency: Signs of systemic infection (high fever, rigors) in an immunocompromised or critically ill patient

monitoring: Improvement or persistence of diarrhea/GI symptoms
Signs of infection in high-risk (immunocompromised, central-line, critically ill) patients
counsel: This is a probiotic supplement used to support gut health and help with diarrhea, not a prescription medicine
If you are taking an antibiotic, take this about 2 hours apart from the antibiotic
It is usually well tolerated; mild gas or bloating may occur at first and usually settles
Tell your doctor before using probiotics if you have a weakened immune system or a central IV line
See a doctor if diarrhea is severe, bloody, or lasts more than a couple of days, or if you become dehydrated
Choose a reputable product and follow the dose on the label

pearls: Lactobacillus sporogenes is a marketing name - the organism is actually Bacillus coagulans, a spore-forming, acid/heat-stable probiotic
Regulated as a dietary supplement, NOT an FDA-approved drug; potency (CFU) and quality vary between products
Spore form survives gastric acid and storage well, improving viability over many other probiotics
Main safety concern is rare probiotic bacteremia in severely immunocompromised or central-line patients - avoid in these groups unless advised
Separate from systemic antibiotics by about 2 hours to preserve viability
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember, or skip it and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose. Missing a dose of a probiotic is not harmful.
overdose: Overdose is very unlikely to cause harm; excessive intake may cause transient gas, bloating, or loose stools. Treatment is supportive (reduce the dose or stop temporarily and maintain hydration).
